in_text_mentions: Electron microscopy confirmed the light microscopy findings: The mesangial cells and matrix showed mild hyperplasia. The glomerular basement membrane was normal. The epithelial foot process fused together with no electron dense deposits. The tubular epithelia had degenerated, and the lysosomes were increased. The renal interstitium had no obvious lesions (Figure 3).

plate_findings.evidence: Severe edema of the lower limbs

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Panel A is a real patient clinical photo of the proband with caption-stated severe lower-limb edema in an article whose title and primary disease is congenital nephrotic syndrome due to NPHS1 mutation (Finnish type). Matches vocabulary edema from birth / generalized neonatal edema. B: Panel B is a real patient clinical photo of the same proband showing abdominal distention in the context of caption and in-text generalized edema in NPHS1 congenital nephrotic syndrome. Tagged as generalized neonatal edema manifestation; distention term retained as proposed finding.
panels.attribution_text: Xie et al. A novel heterozygous mutation of the NPHS1 gene in a Chinese child with congenital nephrotic syndrome: A case report.. Medicine 2023. doi:10.1097/md.0000000000032970. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Clinical images of the proband. (A) Severe edema of the lower limbs and (B) abdominal distention.
in_text_mentions: The patient was admitted to the hospital with a history of diarrhea for 25 days and generalized edema for more than 10 days. He was a full-term normal delivery baby with a birth weight of 3415 g. At delivery, the placenta was large, and the umbilical cord was thick. However, the weight of his placenta was not recorded. A physical examination on admission showed a temperature of 36.6°C, a respiratory rate of 30 breaths/minute, and a pulse rate of 160 beats/minute. He also exhibited facial and bilateral eyelid edema and mild pitting edema in both lower limbs (Fig. 1A, B).

plate_findings.evidence: visual: grayscale ultrasound with caliper measurement labeled 49.0 mm; caption states no size difference between kidneys and no hypoplasia or cystic kidney

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Real diagnostic abdominal ultrasound from the CNS case report (low-birth-weight infant, 3 days of age) showing the right kidney measured at 49 mm with calipers. The caption explicitly states no size difference between kidneys and no hypoplasia or cystic kidney, so the expected enlarged echogenic kidney pattern of CNS is not present; the finding is documented kidney size without hypoplasia, a variant renal appearance in this CNS patient. B: Real diagnostic abdominal ultrasound from the CNS case report showing the left kidney measured at 43 mm with calipers. The caption states no size difference between the kidneys and no hypoplasia or cystic kidney, so the classic enlarged echogenic kidney appearance of CNS is absent; this documents a variant, non-enlarged renal morphology in the CNS patient. C: Real diagnostic abdominal ultrasound from the CNS case report showing anechoic ascitic fluid in the abdomen (red arrow), a direct manifestation...
panels.attribution_text: Misaki et al. Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia and Congenital Nephrotic Syndrome in a Low-Birth-Weight Infant: A Case Report.. Case reports in pediatrics 2025. doi:10.1155/crpe/3135018. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Abdominal ultrasound image at the time of diagnosis of CNS. No difference exists in the size of the kidneys ((a) right kidney, (b) left kidney). No hypoplasia or cystic kidney was observed. Ascitic fluid was observed (a, c).
in_text_mentions: Abdominal ultrasound (Figure 2) revealed ascites, a right kidney measuring 49 mm, and a left kidney measuring 43 mm with no obvious hypoplasia. Owing to the rapid worsening of edema and lack of improvement in renal function or urine output, RRT was considered necessary. PD is necessary for long-term survival in patients with CNS. At 3 days of age, a 6 Fr blood access was secured via the right internal jugular vein, followed by CDH repair surgery and placement of a PD catheter in the abdominal cavity (Figure 3). The diaphragmatic defect, measuring 2 × 1 cm, was closed with direct sutures.

panels.rationale: Single chest/abdominal radiograph of a neonate explicitly diagnosed with congenital nephrotic syndrome in the caption, showing pleural effusions and ascites - a radiographic manifestation of generalized neonatal edema from severe hypoalbuminemia. Radiograph is a real patient image; attribution is supported by the article title on transient CNS in neonates and the caption, though the specific genetic subtype (e.g., Finnish type) is not established (WES negative), so subtype is left null.

panels.figure_caption: Abdominal and chest X-ray of a neonate with congenital nephrotic syndrome showing bilateral pleural effusion (black arrows) and abdominal ascites (blue arrow).
in_text_mentions: ation revealed a respiratory-distressed and edematous neonate with no apparent dysmorphic features and significant bilateral pleural effusions, which were subsequently drained via chest tubes (Figure 3). Initial laboratory investigations showed profound hypoalbuminemia (15 g/L) and nephrotic-range proteinuria (urine protein-to-creatinine ratio of 4 mg/mg), prompting suspicion of CNS. The infant also required multiple albumin infusions. Whole exome sequencing and congenital infectious workup were negative.
